head.title: FKM vs NBR: Which Rubber to Specify for Oil | Margo
head.description: NBR handles most oil duty to +120 °C at a fraction of the cost; FKM is the escalation for heat and aggressive media. But the grade matters as much as the polymer — here is how to specify both.

sections.title: The answer up front

fields.label: Answer block <h2>

lines: FKM or NBR: which should you specify?

parts.text: Use NBR for mineral oil, fuel, grease and hydraulic fluid up to about +120 °C. It handles most oil duty in industry and costs a fraction of the alternative. Escalate to FKM when the temperature goes beyond nitrile’s range, up to about +250 °C, or when the medium is aggressive — solvents, hot oil, harsh chemicals. Between the two sits AEM, continuous to about +160 °C, which is the right answer more often than either and appears on almost nobody’s menu. And FKM is not universally better: it fails in steam, in brake fluid and in the cold.
parts.lead: Use NBR for mineral oil, fuel, grease and hydraulic fluid up to about +120 °C.

fields.note:
92 words · four decisions and one warning, and the warning is the part competitors omit.
🛑 AEM is named in the answer block deliberately. It is absent from every compound selector on this website and from most competitors’, and it is the commercially useful middle step between nitrile’s ceiling and fluoroelastomer’s price

notes: The H2 is the query as a choice.

sections.title: “Viton” is not a specification
sections.chip: 🛑 The trademark point, made once and properly

fields.label: Body
paragraphs: FKM (Viton®) is the material class; Viton® is a trademark of The Chemours Company. The two are used interchangeably in everyday specification and they should not be.

The trademark covers a family of grades with materially different properties — different fluorine contents, different cure systems, different low-temperature limits. A drawing calling for “Viton 75” has specified a hardness and a brand, and left the chemistry open. Two compounds that both answer that description can behave differently in the same fluid at the same temperature.
Specify FKM with the duty, or with an ASTM D2000 line callout. Section 07 shows how. We use FKM throughout the rest of this guide.

sections.title: NBR is defined by its acrylonitrile content

fields.label: H2
lines: NBR: the number that is not on your drawing
fields.value: NBR: the number that is not on your drawing

fields.label: Body
paragraphs: Nitrile is a copolymer, and the proportion of acrylonitrile in it is what makes it oil resistant. Commercial grades run from 18 % to 50 % acrylonitrile, and the difference across that range is not marginal.

More acrylonitrile means more oil and fuel resistance, and worse flexibility in the cold. The two move in opposite directions, always. There is no grade that is best at both, which is why the question “is nitrile good in oil?” has no single answer.

lines: FKM: the same trade-off, a different element
fields.value: FKM: the same trade-off, a different element

paragraphs: Fluoroelastomer works the same way, and it buys its performance with the same currency. Fluorine content sets the chemical and heat resistance, and the more of it there is, the worse the compound behaves cold.

parts.text: This is why the low-temperature limit is the number to check on any FKM specification. A standard grade is commonly limited to around −20 °C. A compound chosen entirely for heat can fail on a cold start, and the customer will describe it as a seal that leaked in winter rather than as a specification error.

parts.text: Low-temperature grades exist and reach roughly −40 °C. They cost more and, in the case of GLT, give up some chemical resistance to get there. Tell us the cold end and we will pick the grade; do not assume the standard one covers it.

sections.title: Where FKM is the wrong answer
sections.chip: The list nobody selling FKM publishes

fields.label: H2
lines: Where FKM is the wrong answer
fields.value: Where FKM is the wrong answer

fields.label: Body
paragraphs: Fluoroelastomer is expensive, so it is treated as the safe choice. It is not universally better than nitrile, and there are duties where it is clearly worse.
Steam and hot water. FKM is a poor choice in steam; EPDM is the right answer there, and specifying a fluoroelastomer because it is the premium option is how that mistake happens.
Glycol-based brake fluid. DOT 3 and DOT 4 attack FKM. EPDM again.
Ketones, esters and ethers. Acetone and MEK are the familiar examples. Worth noting that biodiesel is a fatty-acid methyl ester — an ester — which catches people out on fuel-system parts.
Amines and ammonia. Common in refrigeration and in some process chemistry.
And the cold, as section 05 sets out. Where FKM genuinely runs out — on chemistry rather than temperature — the escalation is FFKM, at a further large step in cost.

Ketones, esters and ethers.

sections.title: The side-by-side, and how to specify
sections.chip: Cost-in-use, kept from the live description

fields.label: H2
lines: FKM and NBR, side by side
fields.value: FKM and NBR, side by side

rows: Very good — set by ACN content
NBR is enough for most duty

parts.text: Cost-in-use, not unit price. A fluoroelastomer seal that outlasts three nitrile ones in a hot application is cheaper, once the downtime of two changeovers is counted. A fluoroelastomer seal specified for a duty nitrile would have handled is simply more expensive. The question is not which material is better — it is whether the duty justifies the escalation.

fields.label: Specifying it
paragraphs: ASTM D2000 does this compactly, and it is the format to put on the drawing. Its Type letter is the heat-ageing temperature and its Class letter is the maximum oil swell, so nitriles typically fall in the BF, BG and BK classes as oil resistance increases, and fluoroelastomers in HK — Type H for 250 °C ageing, Class K for the tightest swell requirement. The full Type and Class tables are in our gasket material selection guide.
Or simply tell us the fluid, both temperatures and the hardness, and we will write the callout with you.

sections.title: The compound between them
sections.chip: AEM — absent from every selector on this site

fields.label: H2
lines: The compound most people skip past
fields.value: The compound most people skip past

fields.label: Body
paragraphs: The FKM-versus-NBR question is usually asked because nitrile has run out of temperature, not because the chemistry demands a fluoroelastomer. That is a different problem, and it has a different answer.

AEM sits between them — −40 to +175 °C, continuous to about +160 °C — with good hot-oil resistance and a low-temperature range that fluoroelastomer cannot match without a specialist grade. It costs substantially less than FKM.
For a hot under-bonnet part running in oil at +150 °C, AEM is frequently the correct answer and FKM is the one that gets specified, because AEM is not on most compound menus. It is on ours.

sections.title: What we test and what we do not hold

fields.label: H2
lines: What we test, and what this guide does not cover
fields.value: What we test, and what this guide does not cover

fields.label: Body
paragraphs: We test tensile strength and elongation to ASTM D412, and compression set to ASTM D395 Method B, in our own lab at Nashik, and those results ship with every consignment alongside a dimensional report and a certificate of conformance. Fluid immersion and heat-ageing tests to a D2000 Type and Class are arranged through an external laboratory where a drawing calls for them.

🛑 One exclusion, stated plainly. Fluoroelastomer is closely associated with oilfield service, and that market has its own qualifications — explosive decompression resistance to NORSOK M-710, and API specifications for downhole and wellhead equipment. We hold none of them, and nothing in this guide should be read as a claim to one. Our FKM work is industrial and automotive sealing.

We hold ISO 9001:2015, certificate 09111526A, Integral Certification Ltd, valid to 21 February 2027, scope: rubber moulded components — a quality-management certification, not a product approval. We are upgrading to IATF 16949, targeted by the end of 2026.

sections.title: Five mistakes

fields.label: H2
lines: Five mistakes when choosing between FKM and NBR
fields.value: Five mistakes when choosing between FKM and NBR

fields.label: List <ol> · each item an <h3>
rows: Treating FKM as the safe upgrade
It fails in steam, in glycol brake fluid, in ketones and esters, and in the cold. It is an escalation for specific duties, not a better version of nitrile.
Acrylonitrile content runs from 18 % to 50 % and decides both oil resistance and cold flexibility. Give the fluid and the cold end instead.
Ignoring the cold end of an FKM spec
Standard grades are commonly limited to around −20 °C. Low-temperature grades reach roughly −40 °C and have to be asked for.
Jumping from nitrile straight to fluoroelastomer
AEM sits between them, continuous to about +160 °C, at a fraction of the cost. Most temperature escalations stop there.
Forgetting that biodiesel is an ester
FKM resists conventional diesel and is attacked by esters. A fuel-system part that was fine on mineral diesel may not be on a blend.
